item.title: REVIEW: Eufy Omni C30 Edge review: Excellent cleaning, poor obstacle detection
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
- Systematic navigation and accurate maps - Limited scope of delivery with no spare parts The Eufy Omni C30 Edge is a capable, reasonably priced robot vacuum and mop with a low-profile, largely automated docking station that cleans hard floors thoroughly. But its poor detection of flat obstacles mean it’s best suited for generally tidy homes. This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Robot vacuums with mops and docking stations tend to be pretty expensive. The Eufy C30 Edge offers a more affordable alternative, with a docking station that stands just 12.3 inches tall. Available for $629.99 on Eufy’s website (with the on-site coupon), it promises a convenient, space-saving cleaning solution. In our testing, we’ll examine how thoroughly it cleans hard floors and how reliably it detects obstacles. We’ll also check which tasks still need to be handled manually despite its all-in-one dock. Eufy Omni C30 Edge: Design and build quality The Eufy Omni C30 Edge makes a solid impression. The box keeps the robot and docking station securely protected in separate compartments. All the parts were firmly in place, the exterior surfaces are neatly finished, and the flaps closed flush. Setup is straightforward. All you need to do is assemble the docking station, insert the tanks, and connect the power cable. This can be done without having to go through the instructions. The robot measures approximately 14.1 x 13 inches and, including the laser tower, stands about 4.5 inches tall. Before buying, check the clearance under your furniture to make sure the robot can fit underneath. It navigated under our corner bench and table without any problems, but furniture with very little clearance remains out of reach due to the fixed laser turret. Its 10.8-pound weight is only noticeable when carrying it to another floor. The docking station is 19.7 inches deep, 13 inches wide, and just 12.4 inches high. It takes up significantly less vertical space than many all-in-one docks. The water tanks can be removed from the top, so you’ll need sufficient learance above the station. Removing and replacing the tanks also requires bending down quite low. The box includes everything needed for the initial setup, but the overall contents are somewhat sparse. Replacement mop pads, filters, a side brush, and cleaning solution are not included. The instructions also mention a reusable dust bag with a zipper, but this was missing from our box. As a result, it’s difficult to estimate the long-term maintenance costs. Eufy specifies a maximum suction power of 35,000 pascals (Pa). However, this laboratory figure is only comparable to a limited extent across different manufacturers. In practice, what matters is the actual cleaning result. A multi-cyclone system sits in front of the filter and is designed to separate fine dust and maintain stable suction power for longer. Whether the advertised 365 days without any loss of performance can be achieved can only be assessed through long-term testing. On the underside, you’ll find a floating spiral brush, a fixed side brush, and two rotating cleaning pads. The main brush is mounted on one side, allowing hair to slide more easily into the suction channel rather than get tangled around the roller. The side brush cannot be extended or raised. For mopping, Eufy relies on its MopMaster 3.0 system. The pentagonal pads rotate at 180 revolutions per minute and, according to the manufacturer, apply 2.2 pounds of pressure to the floor. The right-hand pad can extend outwards by up to 3 inches. A laser line measures the distance to the skirting board and controls the extension. On carpets, the robot lifts both pads by up to 0.5 inches. The basic cleaning cycle can be started using the buttons on the device. The C30 Edge explored the rooms autonomously, first following the edges if the room and then cleaning the floor in straight lines. This means it’s possible to vacuum and mop even without a smartphone. However, the app is required for room selection, no-go zones, schedules, and detailed cleaning profiles. As a result, there is no such thing as unrestricted offline use. The Eufy app requires a user account. Our test unit was already registered, so we had to reset it first. To do this, we held down the two front buttons for three seconds. The app immediately detected the robot via Bluetooth and guided us through the process of connecting it to a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network. A firmware update and new map data extended the initial setup process, but both completed without any errors. The interface is clear and straightforward. In the map view, rooms can be named and edited, while no-go zones and specific cleaning areas can be set up quickly. Suction power and water flow can also be adjusted. The app displays the cleaning route and the current status. After the first run, the detected carpets were accurately placed on the map. Matter support makes it easier to integrate the robot into a compatible smart home. Voice commands are also possible through Alexa, Google Assistant, and Siri shortcuts. However, the robot does not have a local voice assistant. Basic functions can still be accessed directly on the device, but most convenient controls are handled through the app. Eufy Omni C30 Edge: Navigation and obstacle detection Navigation is based on 360-degree LiDAR in the tower, along with additional line lasers. The C30 Edge does not have a camera. Mapping proved reliable in our tests. The robot divided the floor plan into rooms in a logical manner and covered areas with minimal movement. It also recognized doormats and carpets and marked them on the map. The robot navigated around larger objects, such as packaging and children’s toys, with ease. However, it had more difficulty detecting flat objects. It pushed a thick colored pencil and two wooden boards ahead of it and dragged a thin drawing template along for a short distance. The C30 Edge did not get stuck in the process. Nevertheless, its behavior highlights a clear limitation of the sensor technology. Cables and other flat objects should be removed from the floor before it starts. In households with loads of toys, the floor must be carefully cleared before every run. Eufy Omni C30 Edge: Cleaning performance On tile floors, the C30 Edge reliably picked up everyday dirt and debris. On carpets, the robot automatically increases its suction power. However, the cleaning effectiveness cannot be deduced from the rated power alone. Our doormats stayed dry because the robot lifted its mop pads in time. The two rotating pads left an even cleaning path on the floor. The extendable right-hand pad helps reduce the uncleaned strip typically left along walls. Unlike a mop roller, however, the pads do not continuously collect dirty water. Eufy designed the system for regular maintenance cleaning and light stains. According to the manufacturer, stubborn residues may need to be pre-treated in some cases. The robot automatically returned to its docking station between cleaning. There, the mop pads were rinsed, the water tanks were refilled, and the collected dirt was transferred to the dust bag. The C30 Edge then resumed cleaning from the correct spot. All accessible rooms were cleaned thoroughly. Eufy Omni C30 Edge: Docking station and maintenance The docking station handles a large part of the routine work. It empties the dust bin, washes the mops, dries them with warm air, and refills the robot’s internal water tank. The fresh water tank holds 0.8 gallons, while the dirty water tank holds 0.66 gallons. The dust bag also has a capacity of 0.66 gallons and, according to the manufacturer, should last up to 60 days. The actual duration depends heavily on the floor area, the amount of dirt, and how frequently the robot is used. The system is not entirely maintenance-free. Dirty water must be disposed of promptly, and the wash tray, filter, brushes, and sensors should be checked and cleaned regularly. The base tray can be removed for this purpose. There is no automatic cleaning-solution dispenser, so Eufy recommends manually mixing its cleaning solution at a ratio of 1:66. The Eufy C30 Edge is good for homes that are generally tidy. It follows a systematic cleaning pattern and cleans hard floors thoroughly. The extendable mop pads helps clean closer to skirting boards. The low-profile, largely automated docking station and user-friendly app are also impressive. The robot struggles with low obstacles. Cables and small items should be removed before each run. It also lacks a camera for more precise object detection and an automatic cleaning solution dispenser. The limited range of included accessories can lead to additional costs early on. Before buying, it’s worth checking the prices of dust bags and mops, as well as filters and brushes. Given the relatively short testing period, it’s not yet possible to reliably assess their durability or the long-term reliability of the docking station. Anyone looking for a low-profile docking station and able to live with these limitations will get a good overall package for $629.99. Eufy Omni C30 Edge: Technical specifications - Model: Eufy Robot Vacuum Omni C30 Edge T210Q - Dimensions of charging station: 330 × 500 × 315 mm (W × D × H) - Maximum suction power: 35,000 Pa according to the manufacturer - Battery: 5,200 mAh according to external product databases - Navigation: iPath 2.0 with 360-degree LiDAR and line lasers - Mopping system: Two rotating mops, 180 rpm, 10 N contact pressure - Edge cleaning: Mop pad extends up to 76 mm - Docking station: Vacuuming, mop washing, hot-air drying, and water refilling - Connectivity: Bluetooth and 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi - Smart Home: Matter via Wi-Fi, compatible with Apple Home, Amazon Alexa, and Google Home This article originally appeared on our sister publication PC-WELT and was translated and localized from German.

item.title: REVIEW: Everything You Need in Your First Laptop Without the Luxury Price Tag
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
The PC market has never been more diverse, and utterly punishing on the wallet, thanks to the AI boom and resultant price inflation we are seeing in 2026. Most people shopping for a pocket-friendly laptop don’t necessarily care about core counts, clock speeds, or refresh rates. They want something that opens Chrome quickly, plays Netflix without stuttering, and survives a few years of assignments. For a long time, that was too much to ask. I’ve tested plenty of budget laptops that felt tired out of the box, with plastic that flexed under my palms and fans that roared every time I opened a few tabs. Most of them felt noticeably slower within a year. The Dell 15 breaks that cycle entirely. By applying professional-grade engineering standards to an entry-level category, Dell delivers laboratory-tested durability, smart cooling, and all-day reliability. It stands out as a uniquely practical investment for anyone buying their maiden machine and wanting elite performance without paying a fortune. In my experience, cheap laptops rarely die because the processor can’t keep up. They die from everyday abuse. A backpack slips off a bus seat, or the hinge loosens after months of being tossed around in a bag. Most budget machines aren’t built for that. Dell says the Dell 15 has passed 15 MIL-STD-810H tests covering drops, vibration, humidity, temperature swings, and high altitude. These are Dell’s own tests, and they suggest the chassis will handle a rougher routine than most laptops at this price. If you’re a first-time buyer nervous about taking a laptop outside, that’s reassuring. Durability is only one part of the picture. If you use your laptop for online banking or store personal documents on it, security matters just as much. The Dell 15 includes a hardware Trusted Platform Module (TPM) chip, which stores encryption keys separately from the rest of the system. That makes your encrypted files and sign-in credentials much harder to tamper with, right out of the box. Older budget laptops often make working from a sofa or bed uncomfortable. When air vents are blocked, cooling fans whine, the underside gets uncomfortably hot, and performance throttles, turning basic tasks into a choppy mess. The Dell 15 solves this with adaptive thermals. Built-in motion sensors work behind the scenes to recognize where the laptop is resting. On a flat desk, the system optimizes airflow and power delivery to prioritize sustained processor output for intensive multitasking and media streaming. When you move the notebook to your lap, the system instantly recalibrates. It gently shifts power limits and fan curves to keep the underside pleasantly cool and make fan noise practically silent. Powered by an Intel Core 3 processor and Windows 11, this system delivers responsive everyday performance, fast application launches and smooth multitasking across your most-used apps and browser tabs. Good hardware design is about how comfortably a device functions during hours of writing or streaming. Opening the lid reveals an expansive 15.3-inch Full High-Definition screen bordered by slim bezels. This wide display offers ample space to dock two full windows side by side, allowing you to reference research notes while drafting an essay or check bank statements while updating an expense sheet. Underneath the screen sits a spacious, ergonomic keyboard with a full numeric keypad on the right. If you study accounting, manage household budgets, or enter numbers, having dedicated numeric keys saves valuable time. Most portable laptops drop the numeric pad to cut costs, but Dell kept it for everyday convenience. Battery endurance is equally reassuring, but ExpressCharge technology stands out. We have all had moments of forgetfulness, stepping away from a laptop without plugging it in and finding a dead battery before a meeting, which usually spells panic. With ExpressCharge, the Dell 15 powers up from empty to about 80% capacity in an hour using the included adapter while the machine is asleep or turned off. A brief coffee break gives you plenty of power to tackle your day without feeling tethered to a wall outlet. Verified Owner Satisfaction and Eco-Friendly Build When I look at budget laptops, spec sheets can only tell us so much. But what really matters is how they treat you once you unbox them and put them to work. The Dell 15 has quietly built a strong reputation in that department, earning a solid 4.5-star rating across 4,274 verified customer reviews. Everyday users consistently talk about the balanced feel, smooth multitasking, quick wake-up times, and sharp screen, making it easier to trust when you are shopping for your first computer. It is also rare to see a budget laptop pay this much attention to the planet. Dell builds sustainability into the notebook’s core, using 30% post-consumer recycled plastics, ENERGY STAR certification for energy efficiency, and EPEAT Gold registration for eco-friendly manufacturing. Plus, fully renewable, plant-based box materials round out the design so you can easily recycle the packaging when you are done. Choosing Between the Dell 15 and Dell 14 While the Dell 15 is an ideal daily workhorse for home desks, dorms, and stationary office setups, your lifestyle may call for something more compact. If your daily routine involves moving between lecture halls, working in neighborhood cafes, or traveling light with just a slim messenger bag, the Dell 14 offers a smaller, more portable alternative. Both laptops are designed for everyday productivity, but the choice comes down to whether you prefer the extra screen space and dedicated numeric keypad of the Dell 15 or the portability of the Dell 14. Buying your first computer shouldn’t feel like an intimidating puzzle, and getting what you actually need shouldn’t mean breaking the bank. Skip the marketing hype, and you’re left with a reliable setup that handles daily demands, locks down your data, and survives being tossed into a backpack every morning. Rounding it off, the Dell 15 stands out because it focuses entirely on real-world utility. By blending rugged build quality, smart cooling that keeps your lap comfortable, and practical extras like a numeric pad, it proves you can get a machine you can count on without overspending.

item.title: REVIEW: Beats 360 Review: Superb Sonics, With Inspired Design Options
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The Beats acquisition has led to a series of excellent headphones from Apple over the years, helping to supplement the company's AirPods offerings. The new Beats 360 ($349.99) sits atop Beats' lineup and adopts some design elements from the AirPods Max 2 ($549). It has the features you would expect, like ANC, but also includes some interesting new ideas, such as swappable earpads, while skipping a few things that should typically be included at this price point. If you're interested in a pair of Apple-focused headphones with interchangeable components, the 360 is absolutely worth buying. The Sony WH-1000XM4C ($299.99) are another worthy option in this price range, with a more comfortable fit and slightly better ANC. The Beats 360 headphones look kind of like a cross between the AirPods Max and the Beats Studio Pro ($299.99). They have the big Beats logo on the earcups and a plastic build, but they also have the tube-shaped frame and mesh headband that the AirPods Max are known for. The obvious missing pieces from the AirPods Max include the metal build and more premium controls, but that's to be expected. I actually quite like the look of the headphones. The telescoping frame makes it easy to adjust to your size, and while they're clearly not as premium as the $529 AirPods Max 2, they still look quite nice. They come in Black, Cloud, Sky, and Pink. You can even mix and match colors, thanks to the interchangeable earpads and headband. Beats sells two different kinds of earpads: Knit and UltraPlush. The Knit earpads are the same material as the earpads that come with the AirPods Max, and it's a relatively comfortable, breathable material. The Ultra Plush earpads, however, are a soft leatherette. While it's not quite as breathable, I do find it to feel more comfortable otherwise. Beats sells these kits with both the earpads and the headband, and the fact that those components can be swapped out is pretty helpful for longevity. The earpads of the AirPods Max can be swapped out as they degrade over time, but the headband cannot. It is one area, though, that I found on an older pair of AirPods Max to show wear and tear. Swapping components out is extremely easy, too. You can easily twist off the earcups, twist the new ones back on, and the headband just kind of pops out. The Knit earcups are available in Black, Cloud, Pink, Sky, Volt, and Navy, while the UltraPlush is available only in Black or White. The Beats 360 headphones are quite comfortable, but not as much as some other headphones; I actually find the heavier AirPods Max a little more comfortable. The 360 has a slightly tighter clamp and isn't as good at balancing weight on top of your head, likely because the headband is narrower. Still, that tighter clamp does play a role, as it helps keep the headphones firmly on your head even when you're running or doing some other physical activity. The headphones are IPX4-rated, so you can sweat in them without fear of damage. The controls consist of two buttons on each earcup. On the left earcup, you'll find a power control and a button to switch between ANC and transparency, though you can add "Off" to the cycle. The right earcup is home to a volume rocker and a play/pause button, which can activate Siri when you press and hold. You can't customize these, except to select which noise modes to cycle through and a few call controls (whether mute/unmute is one press or two, and whether ending a call is one press or two). Generally, the controls are easy to use, and you'll get used to the button layout, but as someone who uses the AirPods Max a lot, I can't help but miss the digital crown, which is an excellent way to control audio and volume. The headphones connect via Bluetooth 5.3, and they support Apple's Automatic Switching, so you can use them with any device signed in to your iCloud account. It's all powered by a dedicated Beats chip, which notably is not an Apple H2 chip. The result is that the headphones can connect just as easily to an Android device as to an iPhone—they actually support Google Fast Pair. However, connectivity is still pretty limited. There's a USB-C port on the left earcup, but it's the only physical connection and only for charging. There's no way to use these headphones with a wired connection. That's pretty disappointing to see, especially on a pair of headphones at this price point, and given that the Beats Studio Pro did have a headphone jack. Audio is delivered via 40mm dual-magnet transducers, though Beats doesn't disclose the frequency range. Battery life sits at 32 hours with ANC on, which is quite good. The Sony WH-1000XM6 ($449.99) headphones provide 30 hours of battery life with ANC, while the AirPods Max 2 only get 20 hours with ANC on. In the box, all you'll get is the headphones and a soft carry bag that clasps magnetically. There's no hard case, no audio cable, and no charging cable. As you would expect on the iPhone, there is no Beats app to download and use. You'll just manage the headphones in Settings, where you can switch noise modes, change the few controls that are customizable, and activate features like personalized spatial audio. That, however, is about it. You won't get an EQ or other advanced features that have become common. On Android, you use the Beats app to manage your headphones, and the experience is pretty similar. Thankfully, the headphones do support some Android ecosystem features like Find Hub, Audio Switch, and, as mentioned, Google FastPair, so you're not completely left out of ecosystem-related features simply because these are Beats headphones. Beats says the 360 offer up to 1.75x more noise cancellation than the Beats Studio Pro, using eight of the headphones' nine microphones for active noise cancellation. That, however, is a little hard to test, and the ANC on the Beats Studio Pro wasn't necessarily class-leading anyway. Ultimately, the ANC built into the Beats 360 headphones is fine, but there are plenty of alternatives that offer better ANC. The headphones were very good at cutting out noise from a plane engine. Almost all of the low-end rumble and a lot of the mid- and high-frequency noise were completely cut out, and whatever was left over was easy to bury with music or a podcast. The ANC's adaptive qualities were on show here too, as after a few seconds the headphones dramatically improved their noise cancellation. They weren't quite as effective on a city bus, though they still did pretty well. The ANC wasn't as quick to adapt to random noises from things like doors opening, closing, and the bus's suspension, which were let through a little more than they would be on headphones like the AirPods Max 2. Still, they cut out enough of it to ensure that noise wasn't distracting when you were listening to music. In a busy cafe, the headphones cut out much of the background noise from people talking, and while nearby conversations were a little easier to hear, they weren't overly audible. All that to say, the ANC on the Beats 360 headphones is solid but not class-leading. It's also not as natural-sounding as some competitors and introduces hiss into your audio when it's enabled. I would say it's about on par with the updated Sony WH-1000XM4C headphones that were just released, which essentially use ANC technology that was the best of the best six or seven years ago. That said, the Sony headphones don't have as much background hiss. The 360's transparency mode was very good, though. It wasn't as good as the AirPods Max 2, and there was still some hiss in the background that made it sound a little less natural. But it did a good job of capturing the full frequency range, helping make sure that everything sounded natural as a whole. So how do the Beats 360 headphones sound? They deliver nice, deep bass, reasonably crisp highs, and a more neutral tuning than you might expect for a pair of Beats headphones. The bass response is generally deep and rich, and the headphones do a pretty good job of reproducing even the deepest sub-bass frequencies on tracks like "Silent Shout" by The Knife. On this track, there's a fair bit of sub-bass content in a few instruments, but it can lean into muddiness if handled improperly; thankfully, that didn't happen with these headphones. And while they are definitely bass-forward, it's not at the expense of the high frequencies. On "Loyalty" by Kendrick Lamar, the headphones also did well at producing the deeper sub-bass frequencies. On this track, the bass was a little more laid-back and less in your face than on some headphones. They still managed to produce most of the deep bass frequencies in the verse, save for the deepest of those frequencies that I've never heard a pair of headphones produce in full force. Lamar and Rihanna's vocals were nice and present in the center of the mix, too, and the percussion was decently crisp. The smooth, relaxed bass worked well on more acoustic tracks, too, like “Drover” by Bill Callahan. On this track, Callahan’s deep, rich vocal was well-represented, without sounding muddy or overly boomy, and the acoustic guitar sounded crisp and detailed, helping ensure it cut through the mix nicely. This is one area where the headphones fared quite a bit better than Sony's WH-1000XM4C headphones, which do have crisp audio but didn’t produce an acoustic guitar that was as vibrant without some EQ tweaking. On orchestral music, like the opening scene to The Gospel According to the Other Mary by John Adams, the headphones delivered a nice, wide soundstage, giving sections plenty of room to breathe. I did find that the more exciting tuning did make for a little busyness in the upper mids, where things like violins and brass instruments have a lot of presence. But it wasn’t over the top, and the track was still enjoyable to listen to. Overall, I’d describe the audio response of these headphones as exciting. They’re crisp and detailed, and they take a more laid-back, smooth approach to bass response than Beats headphones have in the past. I really like that. The trade-off is that occasionally those upper mids can sound slightly harsh at times. Again, I don’t mind it, and I wouldn’t describe the headphones as harsh-sounding in general. The headphones also support Apple’s personalized Spatial Audio, which sounds very good as far as these technologies go. Apple’s Spatial Audio tech has always been among the best, and that remains true here, though mostly as it relates to music actually mixed in Dolby Atmos rather than a spatialized stereo mix. I still prefer good ol’ fashioned stereo music, but if you like spatial audio, Beats are the way to go if you’re not interested in AirPods. The microphone built into the headphones is solid, but not incredible. When recording my voice in the Voice Memos app, it picked up my words quite well, though it seemed to lean heavily on background noise suppression, which could make my voice sound a little cut off. It wasn’t too bad, though, and I still easily heard all the words I spoke, which is what’s important. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Beats 360 headphones have a lot going for them. I love the interchangeable earcups and headband and the bright colors. Overall, they don’t really do anything poorly. They sound crisp, offer solid ANC, a good battery life, and helpful extra features for those in the Apple ecosystem. The unfortunate thing for Beats is that Sony just released the WH-1000XM4C, a reissue of its classic XM4 headphones. They cost $50 less than the Beats, have a 10-band EQ, and may overall be the better pick in this price range. Still, I think the Beats sound better out of the box and have better battery life. If you’re an Apple user and don’t care about being able to tune your audio, there are plenty of things that make the Beats a better choice. Christian de Looper is a freelance consumer tech reporter based in sunny Santa Cruz, California. With a Bachelor's Degree in Music Technology, Christian leverages his industry knowledge to review audio products for PCMag, including Bluetooth headphones and speakers. He also contributes to Tom’s Guide, Digital Trends, Mashable, ZDNet, and others, where he reviews audio, mobile, smart home, and computing gear.

item.title: SALES: 15 best travel stocking fillers under £50 for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Finding the perfect gift for the frequent flier in your life doesn’t require a luggage-sized budget. Whether you are shopping for a seasoned jet-setter, an eco-conscious backpacker, or a long-haul aficionado, the most thoughtful travel presents are often the simplest: clever, compact problem-solvers that slip effortlessly into a carry-on – or, in this instance, a stocking. To help you win points by not gifting generic trinkets, our editors have hand-picked and rigorously tested a selection of genuinely useful travel gear below. Best of all? They’re all under £50, for a purse-friendly gift that’s still guaranteed to please. These items balance everyday practicality with a splash of luxury – think Bluetooth transmitters that eliminate the need for crackly airplane headphones, smart velvet pouches, and solid Italian shampoo bars that help you bypass security liquid limits entirely. Below, our editor-approved travel stocking fillers for Christmas, guaranteed to elevate your loved one’s next journey before they even reach the gate. Our editors’ favourite travel stocking fillers under £50 Classic Bikini Lipstick underwear (Pack of three) - Ever Vessel Multi water bottleNow there are thousands of bottles out there each promising to fulfil your every requirement – but this one might be the best so far for frequent travellers (the Stanley is far too cumbersome to pack in your carry-on or underseat cabin bag). It also has a number of features other bottles in this list can’t claim, including a tea strainer and optional shake whisk, so it’s as good for your hand luggage as it is for your morning tea and post-gym protein shake. The ultimate do-it-all companion when you’re looking to pack light. See all of our recommendations in our guide to the best reusable water bottles. Editor review: “At 500ml, the Multi toes the line between being large enough to see me through a half-day’s activities and small enough to slip comfortably into my backpack’s bottle holder. It’s double-wall insulated so is suitable for hot and cold drinks and, after a good test, I’m really impressed with its insulating qualities. Cold drinks have stayed that way all day and, while I’ve not tested the full 12-hour staying power for hot drinks, I can confirm that my pre-work tea consistently remains hot for the duration of my 50-minute commute.” Charley Ward, commerce writer - Paire Classic Bikini Lipstick Underwear (Pack of three)Rolling down to the size of a lipstick tube, Paire’s briefs are a game-changer for light packers and determined carry-on only travellers. They’re made from an antibacterial, odour-resistant regenerated silk blend, so they dry swiftly after a quick wash in the sink – making them a perfect accompaniment to warm climates and long transit days. Editor review: “I wore these on a mega schlep from the UK to Indonesia, which required three long flights in quick succession. There was no VPL under my leggings or my t-shirt, and the generous stretch made both pieces more than comfortable enough for a long-haul flight. Travel aside, I wouldn’t hesitate to wear the knickers for a gym class or a full-day hike.” Charley Ward, commerce writer - Katie Loxton personalised slim jewellery caseKatie Loxton has so many lovely gifty bits, and this is a great carry-on only travel essential with space for a surprising amount of jewellery in one sleek chocolate brown eel-print pouch, keeping your precious pieces safe and tangle-free on the move. Inside, a soft suedette lining has dedicated straps for chains and panels for rings and earrings, finished up with a sweet ‘You Are Wonderful’ stamp. - ByMatter Liquid Iron wrinkle release fabric sprayLet’s face it – most jet-setters don’t want to spend precious holiday time diligently ironing their outfits in their hotel room. Gift them this clever spray instead. It uses a heat-free formula to relax fibres on contact, meaning they can leave bulky steamers behind. At 90ml, it’s carry-on compliant, slipping easily into a travel washbag or Christmas stocking. The fragrance is lovely too, smelling of sandalwood, palo santo, and pink pepper, so it doubles as a fabric refresher to keep worn clothes smelling clean between laundry stops on long trips. See our full review of this spray in our Liquid Iron review. Editor review: “I tried this spray on a floaty blue summer dress on a recent trip to Portugal. The spray worked impressively, restoring its shape to a decent degree in under two minutes. It did leave a little damp patch, but this dried down quickly. It is a little expensive at £24 for 90ml and, of course, don’t expect it to do as good a job as your regular iron. Nonetheless, if you’re looking for a completely fuss-free and quick way to help drop stubborn creases in your clothes, this does the job. It’s earned a permanent spot in my travel washbag going forward.” Sarah Bannerman, commerce editor - Nere 5-pack packing cubesMirroring the vibrant, design-led aesthetic of their hard-shell suitcases, weekenders, and travel totes, this set from Australian travel brand Nere represents outstanding value. Beyond being visually delightful (with a choice of 13 pastel variations) and reliably built, they are highly accessible at just £19.99. The assortment includes a small, medium, and large pouch to distribute your items efficiently, though it is worth noting these are standard organisers rather than active compression tools. See our guide to the best packing cubes. - Apple AirTagApple’s AirTag integrates seamlessly with the Find My app, so you can check the location of your belongings from your iPhone and Apple Watch. Updates to the original include a louder speaker and upgraded Ultra Wideband meaning it’s easier to find your stuff from further than ever before, and there’s a location sharing feature for reassurance when loved ones are away – with only approved users able to see where the tag is for additional safety. It has an impressive battery life of over a year, and a more sustainable design made from 85 per cent recycled plastic in the enclosure and 100 per cent fibre-based packaging. See our guide to the best luggage trackers. - Gaiatop mini handheld fanThis pocket-sized rechargeable fan is an ideal travel companion for breaks in sunny climes (and you’ll certainly be glad for it in the UK when the next heatwave rolls around). It’s super light, so you’ll forget all about it in your bag until you reach the stifling train carriage, and it comes with a handy integrated wrist strap to prevent dropping it on the move. The sleek, straight wand design means it cannot fold or bend, so you will need to clip it into its separate detachable dock if you want to use it hands-free on a hotel bedside table – but this does mean that it’s both comfortably small enough for your handbag and can also double as a desk fan – not all personal fans can say the same. See our guide to the best handheld fans. Editor review: As far as fans go, this is so cute – I love the pink shade. The stand also works pleasingly well – I kept it next to my laptop in the office and it did a surprisingly good job of pushing out cooling air. It is a little loud on the highest settings, however – I don’t think I’d be popular in the office if I left it on the top whack for a long period. But it’s pretty, works well, and is swift to charge, too. Charley Ward, commerce writer - Lilysilk Ideal Silk Sleep Eye MaskUpscale silk brand Lilysilk has a range of homeware, women- and men's wear, along with some equally lovely accessories, including sleep masks which are made using their signature Charmeuse spinning technique. There are a variety to choose from, all silk, starting from just £20. The one with the highest price tag (although still very reasonable at £55) is made from a delightful Liberty fabric with a fairytale woodland theme. All of the Lilysilk sleep masks have an encompassing wraparound design for a cosy blackout effect. One side has a glossy lustre and the other, a smooth matte finish. See our guide to the best sleep masks. Editor review: This is a simple, chic sleep mask in ultra-soft high-momme silk. I usually find sleep masks an annoyance, but this one feels like a gentle caress on the skin when in place – very luxurious and the strap is gentle but secure. It has complete blackout properties and I love the inky navy shade, which feels sophisticated. I wore this on a four-hour 5 am flight to Turkey and managed to get two extra hours of sleep; something that’s not normally possible for me on non-red eye flights when the lights remain on. I’d recommend it. Charley Ward, commerce writer - Zucklight aeroplane phone holderMy latest discovery is a gadget I tested out on a recent marathon journey to Australia, when, staring down the barrel of a 14-hour leg, followed by another seven-hour leg, I decided I needed something – anything – to kill time. This tiny gadget can be used as a stand for your phone, as well as hold and attach your phone to furniture via a very sturdy clamp. This means you can attach your phone to the back of the plane seat in front of you, a table on a train or even the handle of your suitcase while you’re waiting at the airport. On my flight I was able to watch hours of my chosen TV shows that I’d downloaded to my phone. Even better was that, unlike the seat-back entertainment, my shows didn’t stop when the captain was making an announcement – which can be particularly long when on a dual-language flight. All in all, the £12 spent was a very small price to pay to have my favourite TV shows keep me company on the journey from Brisbane to London. Lauren Burvill, senior commerce writer - Twelve South AirFly Pro Bluetooth audio transmitte/receiverThis has been one of my all time best travel buys by far. This little gadget plugs into the plane’s headphone jack and connects to your headphones via Bluetooth, so you can use your existing pair to watch the films on the inflight entertainment system rather than the awful crackly ones you’re lumped with onboard. It makes flying long haul so much more tolerable – do yourself a favour and pick one up. Charley Ward, commerce writer - Loop Quiet 2 ear plugsI was dubious, but it turns out that these pretty Loop earplugs aren’t just more aesthetic than the free in-flight squishy numbers, but far superior in every way. They have a discreet design and proper in-ear tips that ensure a comfy, customised fit. Wearing these, I racked up a solid six hours of sleep while flying to Dubai – in an economy seat. The carry case can be attached to your keyring, so you shouldn’t lose or forget it, which is appreciated as it’s very small and likely to get lost in the bottom of your bag. Overall, the Loop earplugs have earned themselves an in-flight essential status for me, joining a tight list of winners that includes this headphone adapter, a phone stand and a decent travel pillow. Charley Ward, commerce writer - Whistles shiny croc passport holderI have this croc-embossed leather passport cover from Whistles, which comes complete with a delicate grosgrain ribbon marker to keep your place and shiny gold lettering, and it just makes you feel chicer when fumbling for your passport at the check-in desk. It slips effortlessly over standard passports, and also helps to protect your documents from wear and tear while on the move. I’ve had it for four years now and it still looks good-as-new. Charley Ward, commerce writer See our guide to the best passport covers. - Elizabeth Scarlett Cosmic Charms velvet everyday pouchEveryone loves an Elizabeth Scarlett design, and this one is surely one of the brand’s prettiest, with golden talismans, four-leaf clovers, and mystical swallows twinkling against a deep cosmic sky. This day-to-day pouch is the perfect size for keeping passports, charging cords, and your lip balm and lipsticks organised inside a tote – or use it as a glamorous evening clutch. - Davines Dede shampoo barSay goodbye to liquid restrictions and leaky bottles with this plastic-free solid shampoo bar from cult Italian hair brand Davines. The formula comes enriched with regenerative white hibiscus extract, for a gentle, travel-friendly formula that lathers up to nourish, detangle, and add brilliant shine to all hair types. It’s an eco-conscious essential for hand-luggage-only getaways. - Antler leather Airpod caseFrom one of our favourite British luggage brands, this is just the sweetest little headphone case, crafted from buttery tan leather. It’s designed for all sizes of AirPods – or you could roll up charging cables or spare currency – with a removable lanyard clip to fasten securely onto your carry-on or handbag, banishing the rummage for your headphones forevermore.

item.title: SALES: 55 Thoughtful Gifts for Men Who Love to Travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The holiday season will be here before we know it, which means it’s time to start thinking about gifts for the ones you love. When you’re shopping for a special guy in your life this year, skip the things he doesn’t actually need and go straight for the ones that count: thoughtful pieces he’ll put to good use on his next trip, upgrades to his everyday essentials, and a few small luxuries that make being on the road that much better. The best gifts for men, after all, aren’t necessarily the flashiest—they’re the ones that become part of his routine, whether that means packing them in a carry-on or enjoying them on a quiet Sunday morning at home. I’ve hand-selected over 50 gift ideas for men who love to travel, featuring many talked-about favorites with a few less expected additions too. From a timeless leather weekender that’s perfect for a quick getaway to at-home accessories that will enrich any guy’s space, I've got you covered with plenty of options he’ll love. Read on for all of the best travel gifts for men or jump straight to the section you think will interest him most. At Condé Nast Traveler, editors spend a lot of time debating, researching, testing, and re-testing all things travel accessories and luggage. If you’re looking for the best suitcase to buy your guy this holiday season, look here. But if you want something a little unique that will absolutely rock his travel routine for years to come, check out some of the gift ideas below. To make his next long-haul flight more comfortable, consider gifting him a comfy neck pillow, sleep mask, or a pair of compression socks. A ludicrously capacious leather weekender or a luxurious Italian notebook are smart upgrades he’ll cherish forever. And in case of emergencies, a good ol' fashioned flask will more than do the trick. Here’s the thing about men: There’s a part of us that will always relish having a new toy to play with. This category is for those who will appreciate a wild card gift and savor the element of surprise. A perfect pair of travel-sized binoculars made from the best optical-grade crystal in the world? Jackpot! The latest generation of AirPods with top-notch noise-canceling technology? Bingo! A smart watch that can track his steps on the go? Perfect! Clothes are a tough gift for the holidays. Everybody is different, every body is different, and a lot of guys are just downright picky when it comes to what they get dressed in everyday. That being said, there are a few tricks of the trade to consider here—when gifting clothes, don’t go too big, too outré, or too outlandish. The secret is to select timeless, quintessential pieces that travel well, age well, and can be styled into any wardrobe: a Barbour jacket, a crisp white shirt, or a navy suit that packs nicely into a suitcase. When in doubt, a pair of high-quality sunglasses in a classic silhouette is generally a win too. Lovers of the great outdoors are a funny bunch to shop for. They typically have all of their most treasured gear ready to go already, so this is a demographic for whom you need to be on your A-game. Gifts for outdoorsy types need to be the newest of the new with smart details, category-leading engineering, and unassailable durability. Think a lightweight Norwegian cooler that keeps drinks cold without any ice (that’s right—no ice), or a comfortable running shoe that can handle endless wear and tear. Outdoorsy folks will say that they can never have too many puffy layer-type things—so go ahead and consider a thick blanket or the iconic Arc’teryx Atom insulated hoodie. And if all else fails you can get them a beautiful Stanley bottle to keep their favorite soups and beverages warm in even the most wintry conditions. I hate to stereotype the genders—but a lot of self-care products out there are marketed more heavily toward women, leaving the average guy in the lurch. He may not know the benefits of investing in a Dr. Barbara Sturm skincare regimen, or how an Omnilux LED mask can help slow visible signs of aging. There’s a whole world of self-care products out there! Here, I’ve gathered some of the best items to kick-start his journey—sometimes all it takes is Dr. Dennis Gross’ miracle-working peel pads. Food is one of my favorite ways to experience travel. If you’re not quite ready to gift someone a trip to sample authentic panettone straight from the oven in Italy, the good news is that the marvels of modern packing and shipping have made some of the world’s tastiest foods closer than ever. A sampler of high-quality spices will upgrade his at-home cooking. A $60 bag of beans is the perfectly fun gift for a coffee snob who might not buy it for himself. And a perfectly unassailable upgrade to his go-to sauté pan (if he even has one), or the investment of a proper stand mixer, are foolproof. No matter what the recipient’s sense of style is, there are certain upgrades that are likely to fit into most any home. Beautiful linen sheets are always welcome, as is a great bathrobe or pair of slippers to remind him of a luxury hotel. When in doubt, the flourish of a Flamingo Estate candle hits just the right notes. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: REVIEW: Creality K3 Review: It’s a Tool Changer, not a game changer
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Creality’s K3 is a solid entry into the swelling tool changer market, but without the lid and TPU Kit ready at launch, we’re left wondering what else this machine is capable of doing. The overly large spool holders impose a frustrating limit on the brands of filament you can use. Still, this is a good printer for fans of the Creality lineup who only need PLA or PETG. - -Top hat and TPU printing kit not available at launch - -Spool holders are too large for many 3rd party spools Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Creality has finally caught up with the tool changer fad, presenting us with a speedy, four-nozzle system named “KliTek” mounted on a Creality K3. Tool changers are the way to go, since they do not compromise speed for color and eliminate the need to waste your filament in the form of “printer poop.” The K3 is still programmed to create a purge tower on multicolor prints, but this is a small fraction of the filament wasted using any type of AMS-style color system. The new KliTek nozzle system supports printing with different-sized nozzles in the same print, which sounds more useful than I actually found practical. Users will also be able to blend colors in Creality Print, a trick picked up from Snapmaker’s open-source Full Spectrum. This method creates the optical illusion of new colors by stacking very thin layers of filament. The tool-changing system works very well and never dropped or misplaced a tool during the review. Creality has tucked 37 sensors inside the printer, with 12 dedicated to the nozzle swapping process alone. No, I’m not going to name all of them, but they do work. I didn’t get a single bad print during the review, even when running at higher speeds. However, the K3 looks suspiciously like a Snapmaker U1 clone, departing from the black and grey aesthetic of the K1 and K2 3D printers. It has conveniently placed, side-mounted spool holders that are a tad too large for many 3rd party brands of filament. We’re not sure if they’re trying to herd us towards a walled garden of Creality plastics, or if they simply didn’t check out all the options. Unfortunately, the Creality K3 needs a lid for printing high-temperature filaments, and this “tophat” was not ready at the time of the review. Creality says the top hat will be packaged with a TPU Kit to enable the printing of super soft materials. The K3 is currently on preorder with a price tag of $849. The competition for affordable tool changers is pretty stiff, and Creality hasn’t brought anything new to the table, which is keeping the K3 off our list of the very best 3D printers you can buy. But if you’re a fan of the Creality ecosystem, it’s a welcome addition to the fleet. The Creality K3 comes with everything you need to assemble and maintain your printer. The included tool kit has hex keys, side cutters, grease, and a nice nozzle cleaner. There is also a paper copy of the quick installation guide and a 200g spool of white Creality filament. The Creality K3 has four tools, each with a built-in ceramic heater, nozzle with a hardened steel insert, and filament path. The KliTek system supports printing with different nozzle sizes and different materials in the same print. Like the Prusa/Bondtech INDX, the extruder and cooling fan are mounted on a single toolhead. The rest of the Creality K3 shares its design with the K2. The printer has a solid metal frame clad in white plastic and a glass door with dampened hinges. The motion system is Core XY, with a linear rail for the X axis and linear rods for the Y axis. The bed rides on four linear rods driven by 2 lead screws belted to a single stepper motor on the bottom of the printer. Parts cooling is provided by a blower fan in the toolhead and a large side-mounted blower fan mounted on the left side of the case. The stock Creality K3 comes with an open top, so chamber cooling is not an issue. Unfortunately, this makes the printer rather loud. The Creality K3 has a 720p camera located at the top right of the printer, which does a great job providing print monitoring from the device tab in the slicer and the Creality Cloud app. There is also an AI camera that monitors for build plate detection, foreign object detection, and spaghetti detection. There were no false positives during the test. Creality’s most annoying design choice is the overly large spool holders. These things are so big, they catch the rim when loading most cardboard spools and simply do not work with spools I had on hand from Prusa, Cookiecad, and Ambrosia. Polymaker and Bambu spools did work, but there’s no reason for this other than to limit the use of other filament brands, which is not good. We did not get to review the special TPU kit, which will allow the machine to run super soft TPU, which is becoming quite trendy for those interested in printing shoes. The kit will replace the CFS Nano material handler with a CFS Flex and add dry boxes for the filament and a special high-flow nozzle. The kit will be bundled with a lid/ tophat with ventilation and air filtration. The Creality K3 arrives with some assembly required. After removing the packing material, you need to remove the four screws securing the bed for shipping, and there is a nice reminder to do this when first firing up the printer. The spool holders twist into the printer’s side panels and are numbered to match the filament slots. Two PTFE guide brackets, also numbered, need to be secured to the rear of the printer with M4x6 screws, as does the bracket for the CFS Nano. There is a communication cable that runs from the rear of the printer to the CFS Nano as well. The tool cables attach to the top of the printer with 2 M4x12 screws each, with the PTFE tubes running to the CFS Nano. The toolhead communication cable is attached with M3x5 screws on the toolhead and M4x8 screws on the right side of the printer. Attaching PTFE guide tubes from the side brackets up to the CFS Nano completes the assembly. The Creality K3 does an excellent job calibrating and bed leveling as part of its initial self-check. Bed leveling can be repeated at the start of each print. Loading filament into the Creality K3 is pretty simple. Filament is inserted into a port on the side bracket, which guides it up to the CFS Nano, which does the rest. The filament waits in the tube until called for by a print job. It is then loaded into the tool. To unload, the tool is selected from the printer’s screen. The printer then cuts the filament and retracts it out of the tool, and it can be manually pulled out of the CFS Nano the rest of the way. All four filament slots can read RFID tags in the spools to load information for Creality-branded filament. For other filament brands, the printer will beep to remind you to manually enter the filament type and color. Preparing Files / Software for Creality K3 The latest version of Creality Print 7.3 is available from Creality.com. It is based on the Orca Slicer and Ultimaker Cura Engine. The default settings worked well, and there is a new AI assistant mode, which is still labeled as beta. At the time of the review, the only thing missing for the K3 was a button to map the filaments into the slicer. The button is still there for the earlier K-series printers in the slicer. The slicer does have filament mixing for more color combinations. A link at the top of the page will take you to Creality’s AI Creation tools and Creality Cloud, Creality’s online file-sharing service. If you don’t like the Cloud, you can export files from the slicer and either move them to the printer with a USB stick or move them over your home network by accessing the printer’s FLUIDD interface. To access FLUIDD, you need to find the IP address of your printer and type that into a browser window, followed by:4408 with no spaces. The Creality K3 comes with a 200g spool of white Hyper PLA. If you want more colors and materials, you should check out our guide to the best filaments for 3D printing for suggestions. For the first print, I was going to run a pumpkin fidget toy, so I grabbed a spool of Prusa orange and was really quite cross when it didn’t fit on the preposterously large spool holders. I decided right then to mod the spool holder with the Creality Pika scanner. I took the scan into Tinkercad and reduced the diameter of the spool holder, then ran the new spool holders in Inland basic white using a .2 layer height and an average print speed of 170mm/s. The print took 8 hours and 34 minutes to complete. I do not usually mod printers while reviewing them, but Prusa Orange is perfect for pumpkins. Below is the original spool holder (left) and the modded version (right). For my second print, I did a pumpkin fidget toy I found on MakerWorld using Prusa orange PLA, Elegoo green PLA Pro, and Polymaker black HT-PLA Pro. I used a .2 mm layer height and printed with an average speed of 160mm/s; the print took a little over six hours. It came out nice without a hint of overextrusion. I liked it so much I decided to print it again scaled up to 200%. Using the same settings, the larger print took 16 hours and 28 minutes and is also very nice with a good fidget action. For PETG, I printed a plate of 3 flexy geckos I found on Creality Cloud using Prusa Carmine Red, Prusa Sky Blue, and Bambu Lab basic white PETG. Using a .2mm layer height and running at 180mm/s, the print took 5 hours 45 minutes to complete. The geckos are smooth and clean, plus all of the links work perfectly with no stringing or overextrusion present. The Creality K3 did not have its special “flex” CFS at the time of review, but I decided to try TPU anyway. I printed some omni wheels for a Death Racer we’re working on in both hard TPU for MFS from Inland and some 95A Inland rainbow TPU. The stock CFS Nano had no trouble pushing these, and the toolhead extruder had no problem with it. It did well. Trouble came when I tried some 90A TPU from Bambu Lab. I’d stick to the harder stuff until the TPU kit is ready. I did get good prints with the black TPU for AMS and the rainbow 95A filaments. The prints are omni-wheel rollers from the Deathracer project of Michael Baddeley. Both sets of eight rollers were printed at a .2mm layer height at an average speed of 50mm/s and each took a little over 4 hours to print. There was a tiny bit of stringing, but otherwise the rollers are perfect. The Creality K3 is a terrific printer that should become more capable with accessories like the tophat and TPU kit in the future. The oversized spools are a little annoying, but easily fixed. The only thing I worry about is Creality’s track record of releasing a printer, then introducing a better “pro” or “max” model within four months. I wouldn’t be surprised if we get a six- or eight-color K3 variant before next spring. At its prelaunch price of $849, it’s $100 more than a similarly equipped, slightly larger Snapmaker U1, which is a tough place to be. It is also the same price as the fully enclosed Flashforge Creator 5 Pro, which we didn’t review, but we did check out the budget model Flashforge Creator 5, which is currently available for $699.

item.title: REVIEW: Lenovo Yoga Mini Review: The Circular Logic of Design Over Speed
item.description:
Source: PCMag
Place the Lenovo Yoga Mini in the middle of your desk, and it's certain to raise a few questions—as well as eyebrows. With its circular footprint, squat profile resembling a hockey puck, and ring of AI-driven ambient mood lighting, you'd be forgiven for mistaking it for a fancy Bluetooth speaker or an overgrown Amazon Echo Dot. Tap its power button, though, and it boots up an Intel Core Ultra processor. Inside this little round desktop are the fixings of a decent midrange mini PC ($999.99 as tested) crafted with Lenovo’s premium design language. Is it as good a performer as it is a looker? Well, it turned in strictly midrange performance, in line with its price. You can, however, find cheaper ultracompact desktops that rival it on value. One, the Geekom A6 Mini, outruns it on some benchmarks for hundreds of dollars less, and remains the budget Windows mini desktop to beat. And the 2026 Apple Mac mini, which we tested in a $1,299 configuration, comes in an $899 model that employs the same strong Apple M6 CPU, albeit with less RAM (16GB versus the 24GB in our tester). Both are likely stronger values, unless the Yoga Mini's circle design and specific connectivity connect with you. The Yoga Mini, which I saw for sale in the US only in Intel-based versions at this writing, comes in several configurations. Our test model came powered by a middle-of-the-road mobile SoC: an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 with four performance cores (P-cores) and four low-power-efficiency cores (LPE-cores). The processor can crank the P-cores up to 4.5GHz, while the LPE-cores top out at 3.4GHz. (This is an Intel "Panther Lake" mobile-class chip launched at the start of the year. The lack of a letter at the end of "325" may be a bit confusing, as that being absent traditionally hints at a desktop-class chip, in Intel's CPU nomenclature. But this isn't one.) Part of the CPU is a light-hitting Intel Graphics integrated graphics processor, comprising four Xe cores that run at 2.45GHz. Also onboard is 16GB of LPDDR5X memory clocked at a relatively speedy 8,533MHz. Our Yoga Mini also served up a 512GB PCI Express 4.0 NVMe SSD. Another popular Yoga Mini configuration is much peppier and—surprise, surprise—pricier. This higher-tier machine offers an advanced Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU with Intel's upgraded, robust Arc B390 integrated graphics, alongside 32GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD. That version was $1,711.99 on Lenovo’s store when I wrote this. The pint-size, circular Yoga Mini looks far more like Amazon’s Echo Dot or Google’s Home Mini than a computer. With just the "Lenovo" and "Yoga" logos for decoration, the Mini keeps all its ports tucked away on the rear and sides. The power button features a built-in fingerprint reader for unlocking the system. With one big exception, which I'll get to in a minute, the Yoga Mini’s design is well thought out. Compact and unintrusive, this PC will fit into your desk setup without taking up a lot of space. Its footprint is about 5.1 by 5.1 inches, about the size of a CD. The Yoga Mini draws attention only with its adaptive lighting, a feature you can turn on or off by tapping the top of the PC. When you enable it, the system uses AI to adjust the RGB LEDs on the chassis to enhance ambiance. It can, for example, emit a light pulse when you get a message, or sync with your music. You can also specify glow colors to enhance the area where you place it. (That might make sense, say, if you put it in a wall unit, attached to your TV.) The system also features what Lenovo calls “Wi-Fi Sensing” technology, which detects when you approach it. When you're getting close, it will wake up from sleep mode and prepare for you to log in. It's meant as an energy-saver. Having the ports on the back and the side of the machine reduces clutter. The rear panel features an RJ-45 Ethernet jack, an HDMI 2.1 port, and three USB ports, including two 10Gbps USB Type-C ports and one 10Gbps USB Type-A port. A fourth USB Type-C connection around the back is also a Thunderbolt 4 port. You'll find a second Thunderbolt 4 connection on the side of the system, alongside a 3.5mm combo audio jack. You won’t find an SD card slot, though. The Yoga Mini's internal fan kept fairly quiet during my testing. All of the air vents are on the underside of the chassis, arranged in a circle around the Yoga Mini’s also-circular inset base. It's reminiscent of the undercarriage of an Apple Mac mini. Here's the drawback I mentioned above: There's no clear way to pop open the Yoga Mini, so you can forget about upgrades. Many competing mini PCs at least let you tinker with the SSD and RAM, so that's a ding for the Yoga; you can always add more storage via USB, but that's not the same. And there's also the crucial question of maintenance. Keeping the Yoga Mini sealed up tight means you won't be able to clean out dust. (You need to do that kind of maintenance to keep any computer running smoothly long-term.) You also can't change out a malfunctioning RAM module or SSD. As for wireless connections, the Yoga Mini supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. Lenovo also incorporates a 2-watt speaker, more oomph than you usually get in this kind of device. It sounds fine, workable for Zoom calls and playing videos. Just don't expect audio miracles; the speaker's not terribly loud, and not suited to impactful music playback. To see how the Yoga Mini stacks up to the competition, I ran it head-to-head against the systems listed below, all mini PCs with relatively powerful hardware for their size. The Yoga Mini does relatively well on price. The closest competitor is Apple’s Mac mini (2026, M6), which costs $1,299 as configured in our test unit. (The base model is $899.) The Geekom A9 Max 2026 Edition and the Asus Ascent QN10 both run $1,699, $700 more than the Yoga Mini, but deliver faster performance for the money. The Geekom A6 Mini, mentioned up top, is also here, as a budget-priced foil. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. (Note that the Mac mini and Asus Ascent are missing from some of the charts below; Apple hardware and Windows on Arm chips won't run some of these tests.) Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess through a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The Yoga Mini didn't look terrific in our productivity and content-creation tests. It squeaked past the Geekom A9 Max in Geekbench’s single-threaded CPU test, but lagged behind in all of the other benchmarks against the pricier PCs. That said, we expected those results, given the Lenovo’s lower asking price. It also traded blows with the cheaper Geekom A6 Mini. We challenge all desktops' graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite.
