item.title: REVIEW: Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Review: Impressive Engineering, With a Few Rough Edges
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The $399 Nothing Headphone (1) Pro sits below the $449.99 Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen), but it has features you won't find on those flagship headphones—including a triple-driver-per-ear design, USB-C lossless audio, Auracast transmit and receive, a physical Flat EQ switch, and a deep parametric EQ. Ultimately, the Headphone (1) Pro isn't perfect; the ANC quality isn't as good as the competition, and the included case is just silly. But it offers detailed sound, best-in-class audio customization, and a unique design, making it a solid option if you prioritize those features. Nothing's transparent aesthetic has always made its products unique, and the Headphone (1) Pro continues that trend. The earcups have the same square aluminum look as the original Nothing Headphone (1) headphones, but with a glass covering over the earcup that exposes some internal components. From what I can tell, these are actual components rather than fake ones, as you'll find on some of Nothing's phones. Whether you find the look compelling or a bit much probably depends on how you feel about Nothing's design language in general, but these headphones won't blend in with the others. At 11.5 ounces (327 grams), the Headphone (1) Pro is heavier than both the Sony and Bose flagships, though still lighter than the $549 AirPods Max 2. Nothing rates them IP52 for basic dust resistance and protection against dripping water; commuting with them should be fine, but you'll probably want to put them away if you get caught in heavy rain or sweat during workouts. The earpads are removable, which is nice for those who want to make sure they can use their new headphones for years to come. Comfort is improved over the Headphone (1) as well. Nothing says the cushions are 50% softer, the headband 10% wider, and its padding 12% thicker. Indeed, I found these headphones more comfortable than the originals, despite their weight. The clamp force isn't too hard, the headband does a good job of distributing weight, and so on. I was able to wear the headphones for hours without issue. They're not quite as comfortable as the much lighter Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen), but that's a high bar. One of my favorite things about the original Nothing Headphone (1) was the physical controls, and that continues with the Pro model. Like the Headphone (1), the Headphone (1) Pro has a roller on the side that adjusts volume, plays and pauses audio when you press it once, and switches between noise modes when you hold it down. There's also a paddle on the side that skips to the next or previous track, or fast-forwards and rewinds when you hold it in position. And, there's a button on the face of the right earcup that triggers your voice assistant when you press it. There's another control on the inside of each earcup—a switch on the left side that enters Flat EQ mode, which disables all processing, and a Bluetooth button on the right. There's also a sliding power switch on the bottom of the right earcup. It's a lot of controls to remember, but for the most part, you really only need to think about the roller and the paddle, along with the power switch on the bottom. You will have to get used to them, since most of them aren't customizable. The exceptions are the voice assistant button, which can instead switch noise modes or control your camera shutter with either a single press or a press-and-hold, and the roller, whose press behavior you can also reassign in the app. You can also select which noise modes you want to cycle between. By default, you'll switch between ANC and transparency, but you can include off as well. The headphones connect through Bluetooth 6.1, with support for SBC, AAC, and LDAC codecs, plus LC3 for Auracast. Dual-device connection is supported, though I found that it behaved a little weirdly. It's actually not true multipoint; it's just a way to quickly switch between devices (instead of connecting to both). As such, it can be pretty buggy. If it connects to the second device first instead of your phone, it can struggle to connect to your phone, for example. I'm not sure why Nothing didn't just implement multipoint. More interesting is the Auracast support. The Headphone (1) Pro can both receive and transmit Auracast broadcasts through the Nothing X app, meaning you can share your audio source with other compatible headphones or pick up venue and assistive-listening feeds. The Sony WH-1000XM6 and the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) can both receive Auracast broadcasts, but neither one can transmit. Both USB-C and 3.5mm analog inputs are available for wired listening. USB-C supports lossless playback up to 24-bit/192kHz, and the 3.5mm handles up to 24-bit/96kHz. Each earcup houses three drivers, which is the most technically ambitious part of the design. A 40mm dynamic driver handles bass, a 13mm-by-8mm precision dynamic driver handles the midrange and lower treble, and a tiny solid-state xMEMS driver takes care of the top end. Nothing quotes 20Hz to 10kHz for the bass driver, 5kHz to 15kHz for the precision driver, and 10kHz to 40kHz for the xMEMS. Together, the headphones offer a frequency response of 20Hz to 40kHz. Nothing rates battery life at up to 68 hours with AAC and ANC off, which drops to 30 hours with ANC enabled. That's not bad; it's competitive for the class. According to Nothing, a five-minute charge will get you four hours of playback without ANC or two hours with it, and a full charge takes about two hours via USB-C. Perhaps the strangest aspect of the design is the carrying case. Nothing has copied the AirPods Max approach here, where only the earcups are covered by the case, while the headband remains exposed. This is a weird decision, given that the purse-like sleeve is one of the most disliked features of the AirPods Max. The major difference is that Nothing went with a hard case, instead of Apple's sleeve design. I hate it; it's ugly, leaves parts of your headphones open to damage, and it looks and feels cheaply made. Apart from the headphones and case, in the box are a 3.5mm cable and a USB-C cable. The Headphone (1) Pro connects to the Nothing X app for Android and iOS. The interface is clean and easy to navigate. You can reassign the voice assistant button and the roller's press behavior, manage noise modes, toggle features like wear detection and low-latency mode, and handle Auracast broadcasting and receiving. There's also a device-finder function and spatial audio settings. As with some other Nothing headphones, you'll also get excellent EQ. There are actually two EQ modes—a "Simple" EQ that lets you set bass, midrange, and treble levels, and a powerful Advanced EQ that goes way beyond most headphone EQs: It lets you select the frequency, Q factor (width of adjustment), and gain for each band, add as many bands as you want, and even adjust the main driver and precision driver separately. There's no alternative I've found that's anywhere near as customizable as this. There's also an Explore tab in the EQ that lets you look through community-built EQ profiles, which is kind of a neat touch. The Headphone (1) Pro uses an adaptive hybrid ANC system with 10 microphones, five per ear, split between three feed-forward and two feedback mics. Nothing claims up to 46dB of noise reduction up to the 2kHz range. While I wasn't able to test those specific claims, indeed the ANC is far better on these headphones than on the original Nothing Headphone (1), though it still doesn't reach the quality on offer by Apple, Sony, and Bose. When it came to things like plane noise, the headphones did a fine job of blocking most low-end rumble and mid-frequency white noise. They still let some noise through in a way that some competitors don't, but it was easily drowned out by moderate-volume audio. This is what the ANC on these headphones was best at—cutting out consistent noise. They still did a reasonable job with inconsistent noises, like those on a city bus, but things like doors opening and closing and other random sounds were let through a little more than the more predictable noise. Again, most of it was easily drowned out by the music and other audio, but you could still hear some of it in the background. In a busy cafe, the headphones performed similarly to how they did on the city bus. They cut out a lot of background drone, leaving only nearby conversations audible. They did better than most options out there, but not quite as well as the best headphones at this price point. That trend continued with the transparency mode too. It was quite good, but not as good as the best. I heard some hiss in the background when it was enabled, and it wasn't the best at producing higher frequencies, which made the environment sound slightly unnatural. That said, again, they did better than the vast majority of alternatives, just not better than the best out there, like the AirPods Max 2 and the Sony WH-1000XM6. Of course, perhaps one of the most interesting things about the headphones is their triple-driver setup, which is designed to help them sound a whole lot better than their predecessor. And, generally, it works. With the default tuning, the headphones sound excellent. They did a good job of producing frequencies across the spectrum, including low-end bass and sub-bass. For example, on a track like "Silent Shout" by The Knife, the headphones produced deep, round bass, making the kick drum sound nice and full and delivering the sub-bass content found in some of the lower-frequency synths without making the audio sound muddy or overly bassy. In fact, that deep bass was coupled with well-tuned, neutral-sounding mids and enough detail and crispness in the high end to give percussion a detailed sound. Overall, the track was a little on the warm side, prioritizing some of those lower frequencies, but not in a way that detracted from the listening experience. That trend continued with other tracks, like "Loyalty" by Kendrick Lamar. This track also relies on sub-bass, but it's much less subtle than on "Silent Shout." On this track, the headphones did indeed boost the bass quite a bit to the point where it overshadowed some of the other instruments in the mix. They did a very good job producing that bass, with all but the lowest sub-bass notes playing cleanly. However, I would have liked the bass to be dialed back just a little. Of course, you can dial it back yourself with the built-in EQ. Other instruments, including Lamar and Rihanna's vocals, were clean and crisp. My favorite of our test tracks to listen to through these headphones was "Drover" by Bill Callahan, which sounded superb. The boosted bass wasn't as dramatic on this track, and Callahan's vocal, which is naturally deep, sounded resonant without being overbearing. What made this track particularly great-sounding, however, had more to do with the high frequencies. The acoustic guitar was crisp and biting, adding a nice rhythm to the track and sounding bright, while other headphones can make it sound a little dull. Percussion like cymbals and drums sounded great too, helping give the track an exciting feel. On orchestral tracks, like the opening scene to The Gospel According to the Other Mary by John Adams, the headphones also sounded very good. There was some slight muddiness from the low strings, but it wasn't over the top. I found that the wide soundstage ensured plenty of room for all the different sections and instruments to have their own space, including the solo vocalist, who cut straight through the middle of the mix nicely. On top of that, brass instruments sounded bright and vibrant, while higher strings had a nice natural tone. So what about other modes and audio features? Well, apart from the EQ, they're not really worth using. The flat EQ switch actually just made the audio sound dull rather than necessarily flat. As someone who generally prefers a flat, neutral tone, I found it didn't quite work as advertised. Then there are the spatial audio profiles, and there are actually quite a few of them for different rooms and environments. None sounded very good. They all made the audio a little too echoey and crowded, which is the opposite of what you'd want from spatial audio. The quality of the microphones built into the headphones was fine but nothing special. The headphones did a fine job of picking up the words I spoke, and I didn't find the call quality bad by any means. That said, my voice was a little lacking in detail, so don't expect an ultra-high-end natural sound. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro headphones have a lot going for them, but they don't get everything right. The problem for Nothing is that they compete with some of the best consumer headphones on the market at similar prices, and it's pretty hard to build features like ANC as well as Apple, Sony, and Bose do. That said, the headphones do have some features you won't find on other models, such as USB-C lossless audio, Auracast transmission, and a best-in-class EQ that will make tinkerers very happy. They also sound excellent and have great battery life, though you'll need to deal with the silly case. That said, most who don't need or want the EQ should probably still go for the Sony WH-1000XM6 or Apple AirPods Max 2 for better ANC and because both still sound very, very good out of the box. Christian de Looper is a freelance consumer tech reporter based in sunny Santa Cruz, California. With a Bachelor's Degree in Music Technology, Christian leverages his industry knowledge to review audio products for PCMag, including Bluetooth headphones and speakers. He also contributes to Tom’s Guide, Digital Trends, Mashable, ZDNet, and others, where he reviews audio, mobile, smart home, and computing gear.

item.title: REVIEW: Genie Backup Manager AI review: The most user-friendly backup ever
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
- Pay versions supports network and S3-compatible online storage Genie Backup Manager AI is the friendliest file-backup program we’re aware of — by far. The AI will help newbies, and the program supports network and online S3 storage. It lacks imaging and disaster recovery, but is otherwise one of our favorites. This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Prices Today: Genie Backup Manager AI Genie, the onetime purveyor of a time machine clone for Windows called Timeline, has moved on to a remarkably friendly, informative, relatively affordable and rock-solid file backup program called Backup Manager AI. If Genie Backup Manager AI offered imaging and disaster recovery, it would likely hold the number one spot overall. The interface certainly does. It’s a step above the rest thanks to Genie’s extraordinary attention to detail. Read on to learn more, then see our roundup of the best Windows backup software for comparison. What are Genie Backup Manager AI’s features? When it comes to basic features, Genie Backup Manager isn’t radically different from any competent file backup program. There’s extremely granular scheduling including go/no-go conditions; incremental, differential, full, and mirror backup; notifications and pre/post run commands; as well as compression and encryption. Pretty much the whole nine yards. There are, however, two not-so-common capabilities that I really appreciate. The first is that it there’s an option to create a second copy of your data in a separate location. Not the unlimited-destinations per job I keep pitching to the industry, but very welcome nonetheless. The second perquisite is that Genie Backup Manager lets you easily create a desktop icon to run any specific job without opening the main interface. Say you have a job scheduled for 11pm, but want to fire it off when you leave the office at 5pm, just for paranoia’s sake. Double-click the desktop icon and head home. Then there’s the AI. Is it really AI? Well, strictly speaking, most of what people refer to as AI these days, isn’t. But within the context of what’s commonly considered such (ChatGPT, etc.), yes, Genie AI functions the same way. Genie AI requires an email address and works off an online engine — i.e. you need an internet connection. You’re also limited in the number of inquiries (100 per month with the Pro version I tested; 40/mo with the Home version). But it answers questions like, “How to backup up to my NAS box” and “What should I back up” accurately, then offers to get you started. Quite frankly, if you haven’t figured out what you’re doing by the time you’re out of inquiries… well, that’s hard to imagine. Along that vein, Genie AI is pretty much for users who don’t know what they’re doing. You’re not forced to use it and I won’t normally, but I do wish there were a way to hide it— it’s the first option in the window. How easy is Genie Backup Manager AI? If Genie Backup Manager could be said to have super powers, they would be ease of learning and use. The interface is the best I’ve ever seen for getting the new average user up and running — by a mile. The language is exceptionally clear and precise, and quite unusually, friendly. Even the error messages are easily understood — a very uncommon occurrence with any type of software. And information about what’s happened, about to happen, and what failed is front and center where it should be. Most users want to check on their status far more often than create new jobs. How much is Genie Backup Manager AI? There’s actually a free version of Genie Backup Manager AI, though it’s limited to two jobs, and differential backup/network/S3 support aren’t included. Note, however, that it will back up to / from SMB locations mapped to drives and two destinations per job makes the two jobs more like four. There’s also the affordable Home version for $39 (more jobs, network, but no S3), and the Pro version for $79, which adds the S3 and runs jobs even when you’re signed out. If you’re running a server there’s the Server edition for $199 with support for Windows server operating systems and priority support. Note that the “Genie prompts” referenced in the price version comparison in the image below are the aforementioned AI inquiries. You shouldn’t need many once you’re up to speed. I’m happy to report that these licenses are one-time, forever (perpetual) rather than the increasingly common yearly rentals. I understand (though I don’t like) that subscriptions software is able to evolve significantly over time, but backup software has to support everything off the bat. Evolving features shouldn’t be necessary for its core functionality. That being said, Genie Backup Manager AI could add imaging and disaster recovery and no one would complain. How does Genie Backup Manager AI perform? I ran backups of all types to local media, my NAS boxes, and even S3. There was nary a glitch and all went off at roughly the speed of the transport protocol involved (10/20Gbps USB, NVMe, 2.5Gbe, approximately 10Gbps broadband). I could go on, but to be frank, there’s really nothing to report, except that there’s nothing bad to report. Should you buy Genie Backup Manager AI? Genie Backup Manager AI is extremely capable file backup, and above all, friendly. Neophytes will love it and other vendors should be jealous of, and take notes on, the interface. The free version is certainly a step up from Windows File history; the Home version is by far my favorite affordable, non-imaging backup program; and if you use S3-compatible online storage, by all means consider Pro.

item.title: SALES: The 10 best things to do in London this weekend
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
When searching for the best things to do in London this weekend, it’s hard not to end up more confused and indecisive than when you started. While it’s never a bad idea to secure a booking at one of the best restaurants in the capital, spend an evening in one of the latest innovative bars on the scene or even explore an iconic London attraction, we’re always on the lookout for new, exciting pop-ups, openings and events. Each week, we get the inside track on exciting things to do in London for the upcoming weekend to help us discover a new area of the city or explore a new address in a neighbourhood we thought we’d already uncovered. Things to do in London this weekend (16 - 18 October) Pulitzer Prize-winning opera Angel's Bone arrives at the London Coliseum following its UK premiere at Manchester’s Aviva Studio in spring. The run is part of the English National Opera's dual-centre model, bringing opera to audiences in both Greater Manchester and London – with productions shaped by the venues in which they’re performed. Angel’s Bone tells the story of Mr and Mrs X.E., a desperate couple longing for a better life who discover two wounded angels in their garden. However, what begins as an act of compassion takes a darker turn, highlighting human greed and socially relevant issues. Address: London Coliseum, St Martin's Lane, London WC2N 4ES Argentine bakery Madre is the latest business to take residency in King’s Cross – and the treats are well worth making time for. The coffee shop at Fabrica X is part of The Mills Fabrica, a platform that supports innovation across techstyle and agrifood, with a focus on sustainability and social impact. Think small-batch, indulgent bites that pair fabulously well with their usual coffee offering. Address: The Mills Fabrica, 36-40 York Way, London N1 9AB A handful of new drinking dens have opened across the capital recently, just in time for cosy autumn evenings spent nursing a pint (or stronger concoction, should you so choose). The Last Exchange is the city’s newest pub, having opened its doors in Exchange Square, a stone’s throw from Liverpool Street Station. The team is determined to ‘pub properly’, with all the tipples you can imagine and a menu of elevated classics. Sip on a pint of The City Scribbler, the pub’s own house beer, and feel the stresses of city life fizzle away. Elsewhere, Bar Buah has started welcoming thirsty foodies at The White Horse, Peckham. Ex-Oranj chef Elies Salvà Ruiz de Villegas is in charge, so expect dishes such as crab caldereta and oxtail croquetas to go down very well with a glass of wine. Address: The Last Exchange, 11 Exchange Square, Broadgate, London EC2A 2BR; Bar Buah at The White Horse Peckham Website: publicanestate.com; whitehorsepeckham.co.uk 4. Have a laugh at the Leicester Square Theatre Enjoy an evening of laughs as man of many talents – comedian, writer, director and novelist among them – Andy Hamilton takes to the stage at the Leicester Square Theatre this Sunday. Cackle away as he explores the wonders and the weaknesses of human memory, touching on the nights he’ll never forget along the way. Address: Leicester Square Theatre, 6 Leicester Place, London WC2H 7BX BREW//LDN goes Bavarian for its first-ever Oktoberfest celebration this weekend, uniting 18 breweries in the same space for two days of beer-sloshing. More than 35 beers are available on tap at the site, found at Riverside East in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, plus a live oompah band, DJs and street food stalls. Address: Riverside East, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, 5 Thornton St, London E20 2AD 6. Pick up affordable pieces in Battersea Aesthetes and art lovers come together under one roof as the Affordable Art Fair Battersea returns for its autumn edition this week. The fair offers an accessible introduction to collecting with thousands of works priced under £10,000 across multiple spaces – with more than 100 galleries participating. Address: Battersea Evolution, Battersea Park, Queenstown Road, London SW11 4NJ Celebrate six years of Michelin-starred Kol, recognised as one of the best restaurants in the world, as the team throw a one-night-only celebration this Sunday. Chef and founder Santiago Lastra is transforming the restaurant into a dynamic culinary festival as four of the city’s most celebrated chefs, including Margo Henderson and Jeremy Lee, interpret iconic Mexican dishes in their own way. Tickets cost £135 per person and include a glass of biodynamic wine Gut Oggau, five dishes, and a cocktail. Address: KOL, 9 Seymour Street, London W1H 7BA 8. Experience the art of French patisserie Claridge’s Art Café has been one of London’s sleekest addresses for a sweet treat since it opened its doors. However, following a rebranding that sees Thibault Hauchard front and centre of the operation, there’s never been a better time to check out the selection on offer. Think artisan coffees, boiled eggs with truffle cheese soldiers and avo toast in the morning, before heartier lunch dishes and an array of spectacular patisserie options until close. Address: Art Café By Thibault Hauchard, Brook's Mews, London W1K 4HR 9. Find hidden treasure at a vintage market As if its array of viral street food stalls, thrift shops and various secret hideouts weren’t reason enough to visit, Camden Market welcomes a new open-air market on Saturdays this autumn in collaboration with Bootyfull Car Boot. Expect curated stalls filled with vintage fashion, retro accessories, rare vinyl records, original art and jewellery – or sell your own wares by securing a stall for £40. Address: Market Place, Hawley Wharf, NW1 10. Get soulful at Soho’s latest live music series Where better to spend an autumn evening than up high in one of the city’s glitziest rooftop bars? On select midweek nights throughout the rest of October, Flute at Broadwick Soho presents a series of live music events in collaboration with Johnnie Walker. Savour a range of limited-edition cocktails as performers including Madeleine (13 October) and Kianja (21 October) bring the soul above the colourful chaos of Soho. Address: Flute Bar, 7th floor, 20 Broadwick Street, London W1F 8TH

Most smart homes grow by accident. A smart light gets its own app, with outdoor and indoor cameras siloed in separate ones, camera footage and family photos live in a cloud account, and a few monthly storage fees quietly renew in the background. UGREEN HomeAgent HA100 is meant to replace that sprawl with one device in your home that stores, understands and controls the things your household cares about. HomeAgent HA100 is a unifying Agentic AI Local Hub that combines storage, computing and control. Supported camera footage, household files, photos and the results of its AI analysis are stored and processed on the device, not only on a cloud server. Local storage carries no monthly fee. You manage it through UGREEN’s UGOS system and the UGREEN NAS app, and it’s designed to connect UGREEN’s own devices (IP cameras, smart speakers, smart photo frames) along with supported third-party products. Security is what draws many people in, but the more everyday appeal may be what the HA100 does with your photos and videos. Automatic backups: UGREEN HomeAgent HA100 can back up photos, files and family data from phones, computers, external drives and cloud services without you copying anything by hand. For anyone with thousands of photos scattered across devices, that alone is a worthwhile chore to hand off. Natural language: AI chat assistant Uliya turns everyday language into actions, memories and insights across your home. For example, you can ask what happened yesterday, and Uliya finds the right moment in seconds, without having to scroll through hours of footage. Separate spaces for different data: A 2+1 storage setup keeps personal files and security footage on separate drives, so a busy camera doesn’t crowd out your family archive. Organization that works like a photo app: The AI groups images and video by people, places and events, similar to Google Photos, but it’s processed locally, so there’s no monthly processing fee. A baby album and a family media library: Photos and videos of a new baby can go into a dedicated album, so first steps and early smiles stay together. Family videos can live in one local library, ready to watch and share. It can also serve as a media server for music and your own legally backed-up movies. Highlight clips: HomeAgent HA100 can create highlights of birthdays, family dinners or a pet’s antics from camera recordings, as well as from your photo library. The idea is that a home camera should capture the good moments too, not only the worrying ones. HomeAgent HA100 also works as a general home controller, which helps with busy schedules. One place to control devices: Supported devices and services can be controlled from the app or by voice, without hopping between apps. Modes and routines: You can use presets for When You’re Away, At Home, Bedtime or Party Time, or build your own automations so devices change with your routine. Spoken answers: You can ask about live status or what happened earlier and get a quick answer. UGREEN’s smart speaker and photo frames, both shown above, extend this. The speaker offers voice control of the home, and the smart frames display your photos and curated art around the house. For people wary of cloud services, the main benefit is that your footage, photos and AI results stay on your hardware rather than UGREEN’s servers. HomeAgent HA100 keeps supported footage, photos, files and AI results on a device in your home, so your most personal data isn’t sitting on a corporate server. There are no recurring storage fees. And when your internet drops, recording, device control and voice commands keep working over your home network. Remote access and phone notifications still need a connection, but the essentials stay up. Cameras are an optional layer, and the HA100 is the hub that ties them together. UGREEN’s SynCare pair covers both ends of the house: Indoor Cam ID500 Pro: 4K/8MP HDR, 360° pan and 160° tilt, baby-cry detection and a physical privacy shutter. Outdoor PoE Cam OD600 Pro: an 8MP bullet camera plus dual 5MP PTZ cameras, IP66 weather protection and a 106dB deterrent siren. It needs an Ethernet run. Both feed one Surveillance Center timeline. HomeAgent HA100 tells people, pets and packages apart, logs deliveries, flags new faces near your entrance and follows a person from camera to camera. For busy parents and pet owners, AI event summaries and keyword search mean you can skip scrubbing through footage. Package detection works best on standard brown packaging. For families who want their memories, files and home controls in one place without another subscription, UGREEN HomeAgent HA100 is designed to make a connected home easier to manage. Rather than relying on separate and expensive cloud services outside of your control, it brings supported local storage, camera management, AI-assisted security tools, and smart-home controls into a unified local-first system that’s a pleasure to live with. UGREEN HomeAgent will launch on Kickstarter on April 13, 2027, with special Super Early Bird pricing. Shipping is expected to begin in late June 2027. With an MSRP of $1,599, early Kickstarter prices for the HomeAgent HA100 begin at just $799. Secure your Super Early Bird price with just $50 for UGREEN HomeAgent HA100. You can cancel and get a refund of your deposit at any time before the campaign ends. Updated November 1: Noticing your current TV screen isn't as colorful or as crisp as it used to be? Displays wear out, and technology is getting better and better every year, with today's TVs delivering sharper, brighter, and more accurate images than ever before. I've hunted down nine deals from top brands on screens from 43 inches to 98 inches, with cool features, excellent connectivity, and built-in streaming software. If you need some tips on choosing the best model, read out our TV buying advice, tips, and news. PCMag's product experts have been testing TVs for decades, factoring in critical elements including black level, peak brightness, and input lag. We use special tools to objectively measure color output and refresh rate, comparing them to similarly-priced models. Then we deploy our extensive knowledge of retailers and use advanced price-checking algorithms to find the best offers. 75-Inch Samsung M80H 4K Mini-LED Smart TV For the best budget deal of the month, you can't top this 47% price drop on a capable 43-inch Toshiba that comes with Amazon Alexa voice support and some nice features for gamers, like a ridiculously low input lag of only 3.1 milliseconds. That said, for a TV under $160, it obliterates the competition. With great color quality, deep blacks, and high dynamic range with Dolby Vision, HDR10, HDR10+, and hybrid log-gamma (HLG) support, movies and shows look spectacular. While it doesn't dominate when it comes to brightness, making it not as well suited for rooms with lots of windows and ambient light, it's more than assertive enough for most other environments. Intelligent adaptation modifies picture settings depending on what you're watching, and the Tizen TV interface is easy to use and brings you access to all the major streamers.

item.title: SALES: This USB-C thermal camera finds home heat leaks, and it’s $57 off now
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Thermal imaging cameras aren’t just for professionals. They can help you identify problems at home: thermal bridges, drafts, unusual heat buildup around electrical components, problems with heating and ventilation systems, and more. Models that can connect directly to your phone, tablet, or laptop via USB-C are especially handy because they don’t require their own built-in display, cutting down on size and cost. The Topdon TC001 Max is currently on sale at Amazon, reduced to $263 from its original $320, representing an 18% discount. With it sporting a 4.5 rating out of 5 stars across 150+ reviews, it’s one of the better options—and at this price, it’s a hard deal to ignore. The Topdon TC001 Max combines two lenses: a 1.5-megapixel visible light camera plus an infrared camera with a 512×384 TISR resolution. Topdon utilizes image enhancement technology that increases the IR resolution from 256×192 to 512×384, providing a more detailed display with clearer contours, temperature differences, and image information. Five viewing modes are available for various applications: thermal image, thermal fusion, contour fusion, visible light, and picture-in-picture. This allows users to either use the pure thermal image or combine it with visible contours as needed. This can be helpful, for example, with building components, electrical distribution boards, pipework, or components, when the heat source needs to be located more precisely within a space. The camera operates at a refresh rate of 25Hz with a thermal sensitivity of ≤40 mK NETD. This ensures that thermal images are smooth and small temperature differences are more clearly visible. It also supports photo and video recording, image rotation, 3D analysis, secondary image evaluation, and continuous temperature monitoring via curve graphs. It features a 50-degree wide-angle lens and can detect temperature differences at up to 5 meters. It can measure temperatures between -4F to 1,022F with ±2% accuracy. In addition, the camera offers 10 color palettes, three analysis modes for point, line, and area, as well as user-defined temperature thresholds with visual and audible alarms. This camera connects via USB-C and should work with most iPhones, iPads, Android, and Windows devices with USB-C compatibility. Topdon says this camera will NOT work with Mac devices, though. No separate battery is required, as the TC001 Max is powered by the connected device. At $263, the Topdon TC001 Max isn’t cheap… but thermal imaging cameras aren’t chaep, period. The USB-C attachment type, like this one, typically costs $250 to $300 for a respectable model. Topdon has a cheaper TC001 base model for only $200, but that one lacks a visible light camera and doesn’t work with iOS. User reviews for the TC001 Max are overwhelmingly positive. The accuracy in temperature measurements, sharp thermal images, and suitability for beginners are frequently praised. Several users describe it as useful for home improvement, while the app is also rated as surprisingly good. However, bear in mind the small sample size of 150+ reviews. If you’re looking for a compact USB-C thermal imaging camera to use as an accessory with your smartphone, tablet, or Windows device, this is a solid option with decent features at a good price. This article originally appeared on our sister publication PC-WELT and was translated and localized from German.

item.title: SALES: Best external SSDs for gaming: Portable performance for any budget
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Perhaps your gaming laptop doesn’t have enough storage. Or perhaps you simply want your game library to be portable so you can move between systems. A speedy external SSD can solve both of these problems. Not only will it provide you with a lot more fast storage for your games, you can use it on any system you wish. Choosing the external SSD that’s right for your needs means sorting through a dizzying array of protocol and speed options. Making the wrong choice could leave you disappointed, either financially or performance-wise. Luckily for you, we’ve tested a bunch of these wee beasties and can offer recommendations guaranteed to leave you satisfied. Built for gamers and streamers, FireCuda X Vault offers massive capacity and convenient bus-powered single-cable connectivity. Vault’s striking design with customizable RGB illumination and Windows Dynamic Lighting keeps your vibe in check and syncs to your rig’s energy. Below are recommendations for drives from 80Gbps down to 10Gbps; scroll below those to learn more about our evaluation process and what to look for when buying an external SSD for gaming. Note that SSD prices have risen considerably since our original reviews thanks to the AI / data center gold rush, and the recommendations below reflect that new reality. The older, linked reviews may not. We’ve also added a couple of enclosures to which you can add your own NVMe SSD, as the availability of many pre-populated SSDs is currently scattershot. Furthermore, an enclosure / DIY option is a way to save money in these time of inflated prices. Why you should trust PCWorld for external drive reviews and buying advice: PCWorld has been putting computer hardware through its paces for decades. Our external drive evaluations are thorough and rigorous, testing the limits of every product — from performance benchmarks to the practicalities of daily use. As consumers ourselves, we know what makes a product exceptional, or not. For more about our testing process, scroll to the bottom of this article. Samsung P9 — Best 40Gbps USB4 external SSD for gaming - Fast and sustains long writes exceptionally well - Runs remarkably cool despite its diminutive dimensions - Like all current SSDs — very expensive Who should buy the Samsung P9? For those who want stellar sustained throughput, but for less moolah than an 80Gbps SSD (shoot, good luck even finding one of those these days!), the Samsung P9 will get the job done and then some. Note, a 40Gbps USB4 external SSD isn’t for everyone. Your PC needs to support the USB4 or the Thunderbolt 3/4/5 spec in order to take advantage — and while cheaper than 80Gbps, it’s still not cheap. If you’re equipped to enter the club, the Samsung P9 will reward you with nearly 4GBps transfers, and at a more affordable price than our previous pick for USB4, the Adata SE920 — which has catapulted to $556 for 1TB, compared to the P9’s MSRP of $340. Of course, with all storage right now, availability is another story. Still you can find the 2TB P9 on Amazon for $650. Besides being very fast, the P9 is (theoretically) a good pick for anyone who wants performance and capacity, with sizes up to 8TB — again, availability being the deciding factor. Some other qualities that distinguish the P9 are its extremely svelte, and thus portable, size; it’s ability to maintain speed even when running very large data sets, while also remaining cool; and a nice 5-year warranty. TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus – Best 40Gbps external SSD enclosure for gaming Who should buy the TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus? With the price of pre-populated 40Gbps SSDs rising due to the AI / data center memory arms race, buying a $90 (currently $76 on sale) 40Gbps enclosure such as the TerraMaster’s D1 SSD Plus, and then adding your own NVMe SSD is quite likely your most affordable external high-speed SSD option. TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus: Further considerations The TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus is bulky, and the style may not be everyone’s cup of tea, but the overtly finned aluminum enclosure sheds the heat inherent with faster 40Gbps SSDs extremely well. When you populate the D1 SSD Plus, don’t overbuy with a PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD, unless you want said SSD for use in something faster in the future. An affordable PCIe 4.0 model provides as much speed as the 40Gbps bus can handle. Note that TerraMaster also makes an 80Gbps enclosure, the D1 SSD Pro. PNY RP60 – Best 20Gbps external SSD for gaming - Handsome, IP65-rated design (dust proof, water resistant) - USB port plug tether is difficult to reinsert. Who should buy the PNY RP60? If you tend to take your gaming drive everywhere, and/or you’re not the most careful person with hardware, a ruggedized external SSD is a practical way to ward off accidental damage. The PNY RP60 offers more than just a rugged IP65-rated exterior that protects against dust and water droplets. It’s handsome and lightweight to boot, as well as an admirable performer, even besting one of the fastest 20Gbps drives I’ve tested — the Crucial X10 Pro — in a couple of our tests. A 20Gbps SSD is the sweet spot in the price/performance ratio for external SSDs. The only issue is that the USB 3.2×2 drives function at only 10Gbps or slower unless attached to a dedicated 20Gbps port. That applies to most USB4 and Thunderbolt ports as well. While a sad reflection of today’s prices, the RP60 is nonetheless competitively priced at $200 and $279 for 1TB and 2TB, respectively. Note that these prices are significantly higher than when I first reviewed the RP60 due to the global NAND shortage. Asus TUF Gaming A2 – Best 20Gbps external SSD enclosure for gaming - Requires a USB 3.2×2 port for 20Gbps performance Who should buy the Asus TUF Gaming A2? Many gamers build their own gaming rig, so why shouldn’t they roll their own external SSD with an affordable enclosure such as the $60 TUF Gaming A2? With the price of pre-populated external SSDs currently reaching for the stratosphere, it’s an especially attractive proposition for 2026. The TUF Gaming A2 is styled to appeal to gamers, especially fans of first-person, military-style shooters. It’s built like a tank, carries an IP68 rating, and is easy to open for installing your NVMe SSD. Asus TUF Gaming A2: Further considerations The TUF Gaming A2 allows you to leverage older NVMe SSDs. Even a PCIe 3.0 SSD is fast enough for the 20Gbps bus, if you find a deal. With those going the way of the Dodo, however, an affordable PCIe 4.0 model will do just fine. Corsair EX300U – Best 10Gbps external SSD for gaming - Magnetic attachement to metal surfaces - Almost as pricey as 20Gbps SSDs currently Who should buy the Corsair EX300U? For those looking for an SSD that won’t break the bank, but is still “fast enough,” the EX300U is an appealing little magnetic square of a drive. That said, $175 for 1TB is almost as pricey as the 20Gbps PNY RP60 listed above. Formerly, the drive was $100 at that capacity. Scant savings aside, the EX300U is the fastest 10Gbps SSD I’ve tested to date, besting the Teamgroup X2 Max listed below by a small margin. And unlike the latter, you can stick it to a metal object like a PC case via the circular magnet on the back. Note that aluminum is not particularly magnetic, so this doesn’t work with most Macs. The warranty on the EX300U is three years, which is the usual for external SSDs, but the 250TBW (terabytes that can be written) per terabyte of capacity is a little stingy. At least Corsair provides a TBW rating — most vendors don’t for external SSDs. Still, the odds of anyone exceeding that TBW limit is rather low. Most of the time games are reading data, not writing it. Teamgroup X2 Max — Best 10Gbps thumb drive SSD for gaming Who should buy the Teamgroup X2 Max? For those who want both fast 10Gbps performance, plus the super convenience of the thumb drive form factor and both Type-A and Type-C connectivity, it doesn’t get any better than the X2 Max. In fact, it’s the second-fastest 10Gbps SSD of any type that I’ve tested. Right behind the Corsair EX300U shown above. While it may not be sexy-looking in the gaming sense, pulling this out of your pocket when you sit down to game is the ultimate sandbag move. Let them laugh, they’ll never see you coming. Having both Type-A and Type-C connectors on board means never having to worry about what type of computer you’ll be using the X2 Max on, though having a thumb drive attached to your laptop can be a bit awkward if you’re lounging on the couch, etc. Teamgroup X2 Max: Further considerations While some gamers might scoff at “only” 10Gbps, that’s still plenty fast enough for loading games — and seek times are roughly the same as 80/40/20Gbps SSDs. Where you’ll lose out a bit compared to those faster models is in the time it takes saving games in the first place. Note that the 2TB X2 Max was on target for a 10Gbps SSD writing our 450GB file, never slowing appreciably or tragically as some do. The 1TB might not do quite as well. The current pricing of *cough* $330 for the 2TB model means you should weigh this option against faster options for a little more cash, and/or creating your own external SSD using the enclosures listed above. A roll-your-own model, however, will never be this portable. - Orico TB5 dock: For anyone looking to add extra ports to their PC and an M.2 NVMe slot for super-fast Thunderbolt 5 storage, this dock does it, for a price. - Asus ROG Strix Aiolos: This 20Gbps NVMe enclosure offers RGB lighting and easy access to the internal M.2 slot. - Asus PA40SU: A good-performing single NVMe, USB4 drive enclosure that makes DIY storage easy, and looks nice in the process. - Glyph Atom EX20: Comes in a good-looking, protective silicon jacket while offering speedy 20Gbps performance. - Glyph Atom EX40: Sibling to the above, it has a similar sturdy exterior combined with USB4 compatibility and 40Gbps speed. - MSI DataMag 40Gbps: Not the fastest USB4 drive, but it’s got magnetic mounting. - Teamgroup PD20: A handsome, tough, and decently fast 20Gbps drive. - Crucial X10: A tiny, weatherproofed drive that can hold up to 8TB of storage. - Sandisk Extreme Pro SSD with USB4: A handsome design and relative affordability, but connection issues and comparably lackluster 40Gbps performance left us unamazed. - Addlink P21: Has a compelling combination of good performance and a striking design. - Corsair EX400U: On the slow side for a USB4 external SSD, but can sometimes be less expensive than the competition. - Seagate Game Drive SSD: Targeted at PS4/PS5 owners, this 10Gbps SSD is very fast for its class as well as attractively styled, complete with a Playstation logo, though it’s relatively pricey. - Lexar Armor 700: A 20Gbps drive that can withstand some abuse — perfect for the gamer on the go or the accident-prone. - Adata SD810: A solid 20Gbps drive, save for writing large amounts of data, where it slows down. Drive tests currently utilize Windows 11 24H2, 64-bit running off of a PCIe 4.0 Samsung 990 Pro in an Asus Z890-Creator WiFi (PCIe 4.0/5.0) motherboard. The CPU is a Core Ultra i5 225 feeding/fed by two Crucial 64GB DDR5 5600MHz modules (128GB of memory total). Both 20Gbps USB and Thunderbolt 5 are integrated into the motherboard and Intel CPU/GPU graphics are used. Internal PCIe 5.0 SSDs involved in testing are mounted in an Asus Hyper M.2 x16 Gen5 adapter card sitting in a PCIe 5.0 slot. We run the CrystalDiskMark 8.04 (and 9), AS SSD 2, and ATTO 4 synthetic benchmarks (to keep article length down, we report only the first) to find the storage device’s potential performance. Then we run a series of 48GB transfer and 450GB write tests using Windows Explorer drag and drop to show what users will see during routine copy operations, as well as the far speedier FastCopy run as administrator to show what’s possible. A 25GBps two-SSD RAID 0 array on the aforementioned Asus Hyper M.2 x16 Gen5 is used as the second drive in our transfer tests. Formerly the 48GB tests were done with a RAM disk serving that purpose. Each test is performed on a NTFS-formatted and newly TRIM’d drive so the results are optimal. Note that in normal use, as a drive fills up, performance may decrease due to less NAND for secondary caching, as well as other factors. This issue has abated somewhat with the current crop of SSDs utilizing more mature controllers and far faster, late-generation NAND. Caveat: The performance numbers shown apply only to the drive we were shipped and to the capacity tested. SSD performance can and will vary by capacity due to more or fewer chips to shotgun reads/writes across and the amount of NAND available for secondary caching. Vendors also occasionally swap components. If you ever notice a large discrepancy between the performance you experience and that which we report, by all means, let us know. Note also that some of the SSDs in this roundup were tested using other equipment and methodologies, which you can read about in the standalone reviews. To learn more about our testing methodology see PCWorld’s article on how we test external SSDs. Who curated this article? Having started computing by flipping switches, Jon L. Jacobi has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two. What is the best external SSD for gaming? At 80Gbps, the LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5 is our choice for absolute best performance. If speed is important, but you want to save a bit of coin, then the best 40Gbps external drive is the Adata SE920. For still-great 20Gbps performance, and a significant cost savings, consider the PNY RP60 and Crucial X10 Pro. Note that the Teamgroup X2 Max still offers good 10Gbps in a super-small form factor. What are the speeds of the various external interfaces and which one do you want? In descending order of performance the current external interfaces are: 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5/USB4, 40Gbps USB4/Thunderbolt 3 and 4, 20Gbps USB 3.2×2 (dedicated port required or it’s 10Gbps), 10GBps USB 3.2, then 5Gbps USB 3.x. For optimal gaming performance, we recommend 20Gbps or higher, though you can easily make do with 10Gbps. Note that currently, the real-world difference in performance between 40Gbps and 80Gbps is minimal. Also, the increase in power draw and heat produced as you climb the performance ladder from 10Gbps to 80Gbps is noticeable. Note that you’ll occasionally see mentions of 120Gbps Thunderbolt 5. 120Gbps is only available for downstream video, not storage or other applications. 80Gbps is the current top of the line. What causes an external SSD to fail? While mechanical hard drives are much more prone to failure than SSDs, it is still possible for an SSD to give up the ghost. Generally it’s the result of a controller failure, although that’s an increasingly rare occurrence; it’s also a relatively easy fix/reset for someone who knows the SSD’s internals such as a recovery service. SSDs will also eventually wear out, though this only precludes further writing to the unit. You can still read what’s on the drive, so it’s not the disaster a HDD failure can be. There were also instances in the ancient past of static electricity bricking Type-A connected SSDs upon insertion. Why does Windows say my external drive has less capacity than specified? This discrepancy is due to the difference between the binary and decimal number systems, their nomenclatures, and a Microsoft miscue. Your 2TB drive indeed has 2 trillion bytes of storage, and if you look at the byte count that Windows displays in a drive’s properties dialog, this should be what you see. This, in the International System of Units (SI/decimal), is 2 terabytes, or 2TB. Vendors use this system as consumers are far more familiar with base 10 than binary. However, Windows uses the newer International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) binary multiples such as 2^10 (Kibibyte/KiB), 2^20 (Mebibyte/MiB), 2^30 (Gibibyte/Gib), etc. Binary multiples are larger than their decimal near-equivalents (one KiB is 1,024 bytes, one MiB is 1,048,576 bytes) so when Windows divides the total bytes by the IEC values you get something like 1.8TiB for a 2TB drive. Alas, Windows labels this as 1.8TB rather than 1.8TiB, misleading the user. Other reasons you might not see as much available storage in the properties tab are formatting or partitioning. The file system uses some storage for file location and size info, etc. Also, some drives come with a small partition containing software so the main partition will be smaller than the drive’s total capacity. How long will my external SSD last? SSDs don’t wear out or break mechanically like a hard drive, but their cells can only be written to so many times. SSDs generally have a TBW (terabytes that may be written) rating, but this is rarely provided by vendors for external SSDs. Hint: They may not use the same SSD inside throughout the product lifespan. Most internal M.2 NVMe TLC SSDs are rated for around 600TBW per terabyte, and QLC types for around 200TBW, though the type of NAND in use is also rarely provided by vendors. That’s a lot of data, and a lot of SSDs are rated well below what they might actually achieve. You can guesstimate by using a utility to see how much data you write to an SSD a day and then doing the math. External SSD warranties are generally between three and five years. As with all such things, it’s a financial risk formula calculated by the company. In this case based on expected NAND longevity and price. As is the TBW rating. Our best guess based on experience is perhaps a decade. However, certain models have had issues long before that — generally due to a flaw or failure in the bridge chip or controller. Exceeding a SSD’s rating does not affect the data stored on it. You can still read that data, you just can’t write more of it to the drive. Should you build your own external SSD with an enclosure and an NVMe SSD? Due to the current high price of NAND, buying an enclosure and populating it with an NVMe SSD is a more enticing proposition than ever before, and it has always appealed to PC builders. Note that even a PCIe 3.0 NVMe SSD will give you good performance in up to 20Gbps enclosures, though you’ll need at least a PCIe 4.0 model to get the most out of an 40/80Gbps enclosure.

As prices soar, you'll want to pick up a bargain on storage when you can find it. For a limited time only, you can pick up a 512GB Samsung P9 microSD Express card for just $99.99 at Amazon. This price brings it back down to its original MSRP and means you're saving $50 compared to its current list price.
